text: The Restaurants theme currently maps most strongly to foodservice distribution and franchise supply-chain orchestration, where route density, procurement breadth, ordering infrastructure, food-safety resources, and SKU standardization can matter more than consumer-facing restaurant traffic alone.

Specialty foodservice distribution is the strongest underfollowed public-market node identified so far; Chefs' Warehouse and HF Foods show how restaurant exposure can be hidden inside specialty, ethnic, or fragmented distributor categories.

Franchise supply-chain orchestration should remain a core node; National DCP is a private/reference example showing how sourcing, distribution, restaurant solutions, and limited-time-offer execution support quick-service restaurant systems.

Layer 1C universe remains too narrow across the full Restaurants theme; next searches should add packaging, protein, beverage/coffee inputs, sanitation/QA, cold-chain/refrigeration, pest control, software, and testing/inspection candidates.
Future Layer 1 expansion should prioritize USD 300M-10B small/mid-cap suppliers with direct filing evidence of restaurant or foodservice exposure and low analyst/media mindshare.

Restaurants theme should be mapped around infrastructure nodes: broadline distribution, specialty distribution, ethnic distribution, cash-and-carry procurement, route-density logistics, cold-chain, franchise supply-chain orchestration, labor/service capacity, B2B beverage supply, sanitation/QA, packaging, and restaurant software.

Highest preliminary bottleneck scores belong to route-density logistics, specialty foodservice distribution, broadline distribution, franchise supply-chain orchestration, and independent restaurant procurement.

Low-attention bottleneck value may hide in specialty and ethnic distributors, food-safety certification gates, sanitation/HI&I suppliers, B2B beverage/private-label suppliers, cold-chain/refrigeration, packaging compliance, and restaurant software/data tools.
Distributor consolidation and any change in cash-and-carry channel structure should be tracked as a catalyst for independent restaurant procurement costs and supplier bargaining power.

Distributor earnings metrics to track: independent restaurant case growth, customer retention, gross-margin durability, delivery productivity, EBITDA per case, digital ordering adoption, acquisition integration, and fuel/labor efficiency.

Franchise growth catalysts should be tested through franchisee unit economics, commodity costs, delivery-driver availability, service times, distribution partnerships, and centralized supply-chain support.

Coffee and beverage growth can catalyze B2B suppliers, proprietary beverage inputs, equipment, loyalty/data vendors, and drive-thru infrastructure, but many emerging concepts remain unprofitable and execution-sensitive.
Need direct filing evidence for non-distributor candidates' restaurant or foodservice revenue exposure, especially sanitation, specialty chemicals, packaging, equipment, QA, and software names.

Need broader company universe beyond cached distributor-heavy Layer 1: packaging, refrigeration, pest control, food-safety audits, coffee/B2B beverage, labor scheduling, POS/loyalty, equipment, grease/used-oil management, and protein suppliers.
Need market-cap, liquidity, analyst-coverage, customer concentration, and filing verification to separate reference leaders from true underfollowed candidates.

CHEF is the highest-priority underfollowed relationship in the current Restaurants chunk because it maps directly to specialty restaurant procurement, premium SKU access, route density, and fragmented-distribution roll-up economics.

SYY, USFD, and PFGC should be retained as reference leaders for route-density logistics, procurement scale, independent restaurant case growth, and national-chain distribution benchmarks, not as underfollowed discovery names.

HFFG is a speculative shadow candidate for ethnic and Asian foodservice distribution; it requires governance, liquidity, gross-margin, customer-retention, and distribution-center utilization checks before any upgrade.
ACNT has insufficient direct evidence tying specialty chemicals or HI&I revenue to restaurants or foodservice; require filing-level customer/channel proof before retaining it in Layer 3.

REBN is better treated as a distribution-dependency read-through than a supplier chokepoint; verify whether the Sysco partnership materially changes unit economics, product consistency, or franchise rollout capacity.

The current chunk remains overconcentrated in foodservice distribution. Next candidate expansion should target packaging/disposables, food-safety audits and traceability, sanitation chemicals, pest control, grease/used-oil management, refrigeration equipment, cold-chain logistics, B2B coffee/beverage inputs, and restaurant software.

Distributor consolidation and possible Restaurant Depot-related procurement changes are important catalysts, but current evidence comes from external analysis rather than primary transaction filings; verify transaction status and regulatory documents before using as a fact.
